country.name: Cyprus
country.tagline: The island of Commandaria, the oldest named wine still made, and of phylloxera-free mountain vines.

stats.note: Approximate; Cypriot Department of Agriculture and Vine Products data put the vineyard at roughly 6,000 to 7,000 ha in the 2020s and output around 100,000 hl. Not reported separately by the OIV 2025 report.

country.overview:
Cyprus has made wine for at least five thousand years and has kept one wine name for more than eight hundred. Residues in Chalcolithic flasks from Erimi, near Limassol, analysed in 2005, point to wine around 3500 BC, and the Bronze Age site of Pyrgos-Mavroraki had a winery beside its perfume workshop. Hesiod described drying grapes in the sun before making sweet wine, the method still used in the island's great dessert wine, Commandaria.

Commandaria takes its name from the Grande Commanderie, the estate around Kolossi castle held by the Knights Templar and then the Knights Hospitaller from the late twelfth century. The knights shipped the sweet amber wine to Europe's courts and to pilgrims bound for the Holy Land, which is why Commandaria claims to be the oldest named wine still in production. Legend adds that Richard the Lionheart called it 'the wine of kings and the king of wines' at his wedding in Limassol in 1191, and that a sweet Cypriot wine, widely believed to be Commandaria, won 'La Bataille des Vins', the tasting staged by the French king and recorded in Henri d'Andeli's poem of about 1224. In December 2025 UNESCO inscribed Commandaria's traditions in the 14 villages on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The modern industry was built on volume. British rule after 1878, the island's freedom from phylloxera (strict quarantine kept the louse out) and cheap fortified 'Cyprus sherry' made Cyprus one of Britain's leading wine suppliers by the 1960s, while big Limassol companies (KEO, ETKO, LOEL, SODAP) shipped bulk wine to the Soviet bloc. When those markets collapsed in the 1980s and 1990s, the state paid for small regional wineries in the Troodos villages, and the island began bottling its own grapes: the red Maratheftiko and Yiannoudi, the white Xynisteri and Promara, alongside the workhorse Mavro.

Today about 50 to 60 wineries work mostly on the southern slopes of the Troodos mountains, between 600 and 1,500 metres, where vines grow on their own roots in limestone, chalk and volcanic soils. The island has seven PDOs: Commandaria plus six regional zones (Pitsilia, Vouni Panagias-Ambelitis, Laona Akama and the three Krasochoria Lemesou zones). The island's division since 1974 means all of the PDOs lie in the south; the north has a few vineyards but no EU-registered appellations.

history.title: Wine in Erimi's flasks
history.text: Chalcolithic round-bottomed flasks excavated at Erimi in the 1930s were analysed in 2005 and showed traces consistent with wine, among the earliest in the Mediterranean. The Cyprus Wine Museum stands in the village.

history.title: Pyrgos-Mavroraki winery
history.text: Excavations at Pyrgos-Mavroraki in the Limassol hills found a Bronze Age industrial complex with a perfumery, an olive press and a winery with grape seeds and storage vessels.

history.title: Hesiod's sun-dried grapes
history.text: Hesiod's Works and Days describes laying grapes in the sun for ten days before pressing, the technique still used for Commandaria.

history.title: Richard the Lionheart in Limassol
history.text: Richard I married Berengaria of Navarre in Limassol; tradition says he praised the island's sweet wine as 'the wine of kings and the king of wines'. He then sold Cyprus to the Templars.

history.title: The Battle of the Wines
history.text: Henri d'Andeli's poem La Bataille des Vins records a tasting held for the French king; the winner was a sweet wine of Cyprus, traditionally identified as Commandaria.

history.title: The Grande Commanderie at Kolossi
history.text: The Knights Hospitaller ran their main Cypriot estate from Kolossi castle (the present keep dates from 1454) and shipped its sweet wine to Europe, giving Commandaria its name.

history.title: Phylloxera-free boom and Cyprus sherry
history.text: Under British rule and with European vineyards destroyed by phylloxera, Cyprus exported grapes and wine; 'Cyprus sherry', first sold under that name in 1937, made the island Britain's third-biggest wine supplier by the 1960s.

history.title: Commandaria's appellation law
history.text: A law of 2 March 1990 limited Commandaria to 14 villages on the southern slopes of the Troodos; the EU registered it as a PDO.

history.title: UNESCO recognises Commandaria
history.text: In December 2025 UNESCO inscribed Commandaria wine and its traditions on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, Cyprus's seventh element on the list.

country.classification: Cyprus follows the EU system: seven PDOs (ΠΟΠ, OEOP on older labels) and four regional PGIs named after the districts (Lemesos, Pafos, Larnaka, Lefkosia). Commandaria's rules are among the strictest in Europe: only Xynisteri and Mavro from 14 named villages, goblet-trained and unirrigated vines at least four years old, harvest only when the Vine Products Commission gives the signal, grapes sun-dried (usually 7 to 10 days) to 390 to 450 grams of sugar per litre, and at least two years in oak. The six regional PDOs require vineyards above about 600 to 750 metres, low yields and minimum vine ages.
country.climate_soils: A hot, dry Mediterranean island climate is cooled by altitude: the Troodos range rises to 1,952 metres at Mount Olympus, and almost all quality vineyards sit on its southern and western slopes between 400 and 1,500 metres. Soils are chalk and limestone (Laona, the Krasochoria), with igneous and volcanic soils on the higher Troodos (Pitsilia). Phylloxera has never reached Cyprus, so vines grow ungrafted.

grapes.name: Mavro
grapes.note: The most planted red, high-yielding and rustic, but the essential partner in Commandaria.

grapes.name: Xynisteri
grapes.note: The main white: fresh, citrus and saline at altitude; the other Commandaria grape.

grapes.name: Maratheftiko
grapes.note: Deep-coloured, structured native red, the island's flagship for quality reds (needs a pollinator: the flowers are functionally female).

grapes.name: Yiannoudi
grapes.note: Rare native red rediscovered in the 2000s, fresh and spicy.

grapes.name: Promara
grapes.note: Rescued native white, aromatic and fresh.

grapes.name: Spourtiko and Morokanella
grapes.note: Rare native whites, part of the revival.

further_reading: Commandaria: The Wine of Kings, Yiannis Mozoras (various editions)
Wine Grapes, Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding and José Vouillamoz

regions.name: Troodos wine villages
regions.tagline: The 'wine villages' of the southern Troodos, from Commandaria to Pitsilia.
regions.summary: Almost all Cypriot quality wine comes from the southern and western slopes of the Troodos, in the Limassol and Paphos districts. Here are the 14 Commandaria villages, the Krasochoria Lemesou (wine villages of Limassol) around Omodos, Vasa and Koilani, the high Pitsilia area to the east, and in Paphos the Vouni Panagias plateau and the Laona-Akama peninsula.
regions.history: Small regional wineries were subsidised from the 1980s to move winemaking out of the Limassol port factories and into the villages, cutting the distance hot grapes travelled.
regions.terroir: Altitudes of 400 to 1,500 metres; chalk, limestone and volcanic soils; unirrigated ungrafted bush vines.
regions.grapes: Xynisteri, Mavro, Maratheftiko, Yiannoudi, Promara, international varieties.
regions.styles: Fresh whites, structured reds, sweet Commandaria.

cy-commandaria.name: Commandaria
cy-commandaria.summary:
Commandaria is a sweet amber wine made from sun-dried Xynisteri and Mavro grown in 14 villages on the southern slopes of the Troodos, north of Limassol: Agios Georgios, Agios Konstantinos, Agios Mamas, Agios Pavlos, Apsiou, Gerasa, Doros, Zoopigi, Kalo Chorio, Kapilio, Laneia, Louvaras, Monagri and Silikou. Grapes are picked very ripe, laid in the sun for about a week to raise sugar to 390 to 450 grams per litre, fermented until the yeast gives up around 15 percent alcohol (fortification is allowed but not required), and aged at least two years in oak. Good Commandaria tastes of raisin, fig, carob, coffee and orange peel with enough acidity to stay fresh, and old bottlings from the solera-like 'mana' tradition can be remarkable.

The name comes from the Grande Commanderie of the Knights Templar and Hospitaller at Kolossi, which exported the wine across medieval Europe, and it is the oldest wine name in continuous use. Production fell to around 200,000 bottles a year by 2025; UNESCO's inscription of its traditions in December 2025 is meant to help revive it.
cy-commandaria.terroir: South-facing slopes of 500 to 900 metres; calcareous and volcanic soils; goblet-trained, unirrigated vines at least four years old.
cy-commandaria.nerd_note: Many old Commandaria lots were kept in a 'mana' (mother) jar, topped up with each new vintage like a solera, so a single jar could hold wine generations old.

cy-krasochoria-lemesou.name: Krasochoria Lemesou
cy-krasochoria-lemesou.grapes: Xynisteri, Maratheftiko, Mavro, Yiannoudi, Promara and international varieties
cy-krasochoria-lemesou.summary: The 'wine villages of Limassol' PDO covers the high villages west of the Commandaria zone, around Omodos, Vasa, Koilani, Malia and Arsos, the historic heart of Cypriot table wine. Limestone and chalk soils at 600 to 1,200 metres give fresh Xynisteri and structured Maratheftiko.

cy-krasochoria-lemesou-afames.name: Krasochoria Lemesou-Afames
cy-krasochoria-lemesou-afames.summary: A sub-zone of the Limassol wine villages named after the Afames hill above Pelendri and Kato Platres, on the higher, volcanic eastern side of the zone. Higher and cooler than most of the Limassol wine villages, it is planted with Xynisteri, Maratheftiko and Mavro alongside international grapes.

cy-krasochoria-lemesou-laona.name: Krasochoria Lemesou-Laona
cy-krasochoria-lemesou-laona.summary: A sub-zone of the Limassol wine villages around the Laona area near Arsos and Omodos, on limestone at 900 to 1,200 metres. The limestone gives fresh, saline Xynisteri, and Maratheftiko and Yiannoudi give the zone's best reds.

cy-laona-akama.name: Laona Akama
cy-laona-akama.grapes: Xynisteri, Maratheftiko, Mavro, Yiannoudi and others
cy-laona-akama.summary: The limestone Laona plateau above the Akamas peninsula in the north-west, around Kathikas and Kritou Terra, between 450 and 750 metres; sea breezes give some of the island's most saline whites.

cy-pitsilia.name: Pitsilia
cy-pitsilia.grapes: Xynisteri, Maratheftiko, Mavro, Cabernet Sauvignon and others
cy-pitsilia.summary: The high Pitsilia area on the eastern Troodos (around Kyperounda, Agros and Pelendri) has some of Europe's highest vineyards, up to around 1,500 metres, on igneous soils. Kyperounda's winery at about 1,450 metres is among the highest in Europe.

cy-vouni-panagias-ampelitis.name: Vouni Panagias-Ambelitis
cy-vouni-panagias-ampelitis.summary: A cool plateau around Panagia in the Paphos hills at 800 to 1,100 metres, the source of fresh Xynisteri and of Maratheftiko from Vouni Panagia winery. The plateau is among the coolest places to grow grapes in Cyprus, and the zone's bush vines are ungrafted, like all Cypriot vines.

sites.name: Kolossi Castle
sites.text: The keep of the Grande Commanderie of the Knights Hospitaller, rebuilt in 1454 on an earlier crusader castle west of Limassol. From here the knights ran the estates whose sweet wine took the name Commandaria; a medieval sugar mill stands beside it.

sites.name: Cyprus Wine Museum, Erimi
sites.text: A museum in the village of Erimi, where Chalcolithic flasks with wine residues of about 3500 BC were found, telling the story of 5,500 years of Cypriot wine.

sites.name: Pyrgos-Mavroraki
sites.text: Bronze Age industrial site of about 2000 BC in the Limassol hills, with a perfumery, olive press and winery that yielded grape seeds and wine jars.

sites.name: Omodos
sites.text: The best-known of the Limassol wine villages, around the Timios Stavros monastery, with an old communal wine press (linos) and many small wineries.

sites.name: Kyperounda Winery
sites.text: One of the highest wineries in Europe, at around 1,450 metres in Pitsilia; makes Xynisteri, Petritis and Commandaria.

sites.name: Zoopigi
sites.text: One of the 14 villages entitled to make Commandaria under the 1990 law, high in the hills north of Limassol. Growers here leave Xynisteri and Mavro to over-ripen on goblet-trained, unirrigated vines, then dry the bunches in the sun before pressing.

sites.name: Kalo Chorio (Limassol)
sites.text: Commandaria village in the hills north of Limassol and one of the centres of the traditional sweet-wine trade. Grapes are laid out on roofs and terraces for about a week to concentrate their sugar before pressing, the method Hesiod described almost three thousand years ago.

sites.name: Doros
sites.text: One of the 14 Commandaria villages, on the slopes of the Kouris valley at around 500 to 800 metres. Small producers here keep the tradition of fermenting sun-dried Mavro and Xynisteri until the yeast stops naturally at about 15 percent alcohol.

sites.name: Laneia
sites.text: A stone-built Commandaria village above the Kouris river, with a restored traditional wine press and old cellar houses. Its terraces of bush-trained Mavro and Xynisteri are part of the zone protected by the 1990 Commandaria law.

sites.name: Monagri
sites.text: Commandaria village on the slopes of the Kouris valley, known for its Byzantine monastery of Panagia Amasgou. The south-facing terraces catch full sun, ideal for drying grapes.

sites.name: Kathikas
sites.text: Village on the limestone Laona plateau above the Akamas peninsula, at the centre of the Laona Akama PDO. Several small wineries here make saline Xynisteri and Maratheftiko from vineyards at around 600 metres that catch the sea breeze.

sites.name: Koilani
sites.text: One of the Limassol wine villages on the southern Troodos, with old stone wine presses and a small church museum. Its high vineyards supply the Krasochoria Lemesou PDO, mostly Xynisteri and Mavro on limestone and chalk.
